## Sound history

Semitic root-and-pattern morphology organizes much Aramaic vocabulary, alongside affixal morphology. Historical varieties show changes in emphatic consonants, gutturals, vowels, and consonant clusters; outcomes vary by branch and period. Transliteration conventions differ in representing emphatics, spirantization, vowel length, and matres lectionis, so a sound history must specify dialect and script tradition.

For reliable sound-change claims, identify the source stage, daughter branch, conditioning environment, and counterexamples. Orthographic similarity alone cannot establish cognacy or sound correspondence. Reconstructed segments use an asterisk and remain hypotheses.

## Syllables, prosody, and syntax

Aramaic clause order varies by period, genre, and discourse; verb-subject-object and subject-verb-object patterns are both represented in descriptions. Semitic syllables typically center on a vowel nucleus and allow consonant clusters/codas, with dialect-specific restrictions. Tense-aspect systems and periphrastic constructions shift across the long record; an Imperial text cannot stand for all modern dialects.

The descriptive labels here are broad summaries, not templates for every dialect or genre. Compare attested forms by date and register; syntax may change while a writing convention remains conservative. Phonological syllables, script units, aksharas, and Unicode grapheme clusters are distinct analytical units.

## Script, Unicode, diacritics, and glyphs

The Aramaic consonantal alphabet is written right-to-left. Old Aramaic inscriptional forms gave way to a widely used Imperial/official chancery hand; after imperial standardization weakened, regional cursive and monumental styles diverged. The tradition became a source for Jewish square script, Palmyrene, Syriac, Mandaic, and Nabataean; Nabataean script development is important to Arabic script history. Descendant scripts are related but not interchangeable: ductus, ligatures, letterforms, and later vowel pointing differ by community and period.

**Unicode model:** Imperial Aramaic U+10840–U+1085F is encoded separately from Hebrew, Syriac, Nabataean, Palmyrene, and other related scripts. Text direction is right-to-left.

| Sample | Code points | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 𐡀 | U+10840 | Imperial Aramaic Aleph |
| 𐡁 | U+10841 | Imperial Aramaic Beth |
| 𐡂 | U+10842 | Imperial Aramaic Gimel |
| 𐡃 | U+10843 | Imperial Aramaic Daleth |

**Subscripts:** No productive subscript alphabet in Imperial Aramaic. Scholarly transliteration may use subscript numerals or dots as editorial notation; those are not Aramaic script characters.

**Diacritics and combining marks:** Early abjads generally leave short vowels unwritten; later script traditions developed distinct pointing systems. These vowel marks are tradition-specific and must not be projected backward onto Imperial Aramaic. Combining marks in later Syriac/Hebrew text have their own Unicode blocks and ordering rules.

**Glyph strokes and layout:** Unicode encodes character identity and text order, not ductus. Paleographic letterforms evolve through inscriptions and manuscripts; code point identity does not prescribe historical stroke order.

Unicode encodes characters, not the complete historical calligraphic or palaeographic process. Record source form, normalization, transliteration, and rendering assumptions separately.

entries.content:
## Family placement

Ancient Egyptian is a distinct branch of Afroasiatic, not a sister dialect of Arabic or Hebrew. Its recorded stages are conventionally Old Egyptian, Middle Egyptian, Late Egyptian, Demotic, and Coptic, each reflecting chronological and register differences. Comparative Afroasiatic ties link Egyptian with Semitic, Berber, Cushitic, Chadic, and other groupings, but deep subgroup relationships and the proto-language date are debated.

**Proposed root:** Proto-Afroasiatic (deep reconstructed ancestor; Egyptian is one daughter branch) — 8000–15000 BP, using 1950 CE as the conventional BP origin. The qualifying point estimate is 8000 BP. Confidence: very low for exact deep dates and homeland; proposed dates differ by millennia. This date concerns the stated ancestor; it is not an age claim for the modern language. 

**Siblings and comparisons:**
- Semitic languages (distinct Afroasiatic branch; includes Aramaic, Hebrew, Arabic)
- Berber/Amazigh languages (distinct Afroasiatic branch)
- Cushitic languages (distinct Afroasiatic branch)
- Chadic languages (distinct Afroasiatic branch)
- Omotic languages (classification debated)

Do not flatten distant relatives and immediate sister groups into a single branching level.

## Sources

## Chronology and evidence

Hieroglyphic writing appears in Egypt by the end of the fourth millennium BCE, with fully developed textual evidence by the early dynastic/Old Kingdom periods. The language stages extend from Old Egyptian through Coptic, which remained spoken into the medieval period and survives liturgically. Dating a script, a text, and a reconstructed ancestor are distinct tasks.

**Dating statement:** Published Proto-Afroasiatic chronology proposals vary widely: some place it around 8,000–10,000 years ago and others at 15,000 years or more. The 8,000 BP value is the younger edge of the cited proposals, not a consensus estimate; Egyptian hieroglyphic attestation is a separate datum.

Keep three clocks separate: (1) reconstructed ancestor age, (2) earliest surviving written attestation, and (3) emergence of a standardized modern variety. They answer different questions. A lack of early writing is not evidence that a language did not exist.

## Sound history

Egyptian writing often omits vowels, so the phonology of many stages is reconstructed with uncertainty. Consonantal changes, weakening/loss of final consonants, and changes in verbal morphology help distinguish stages; Coptic, written with an alphabetic Greek-derived script supplemented by Egyptian signs, makes vowels more visible. Conventional Egyptological transliteration is not itself a direct recording of ancient pronunciation.

For reliable sound-change claims, identify the source stage, daughter branch, conditioning environment, and counterexamples. Orthographic similarity alone cannot establish cognacy or sound correspondence. Reconstructed segments use an asterisk and remain hypotheses.

## Syllables, prosody, and syntax

Egyptian syntax changes substantially through its stages: word order, verbal constructions, and clause-linking strategies develop over millennia. Old and Middle Egyptian can show verb-initial patterns in particular constructions, while later Egyptian and Coptic restructure verbal and analytic constructions. Syllable structure is reconstructed cautiously from consonantal scripts and later Coptic evidence; do not treat a transliteration as phonetic syllabification.

The descriptive labels here are broad summaries, not templates for every dialect or genre. Compare attested forms by date and register; syntax may change while a writing convention remains conservative. Phonological syllables, script units, aksharas, and Unicode grapheme clusters are distinct analytical units.

## Script, Unicode, diacritics, and glyphs

Egyptian language used successive and partly overlapping scripts: monumental hieroglyphs, cursive hieratic, later Demotic, and Coptic. Hieratic is a cursive hieroglyphic hand; Demotic developed as an increasingly cursive administrative/literary script; Coptic uses Greek letters plus signs derived from Demotic for Egyptian sounds absent from Greek. Sign shapes, orientation toward people/animals, and group placement in quadrats vary with medium and period. Unicode logical order and layout controls are not a facsimile of the historical writing surface.

**Unicode model:** Egyptian Hieroglyphs U+13000–U+1342F; Egyptian Hieroglyph Format Controls U+13430–U+1345F; Egyptian Hieroglyphs Extended-A U+13460–U+143FF. Unicode encodes signs and controls for grouping/formatting, not a complete facsimile of manuscript layout.

| Sample | Code points | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 𓀀 | U+13000 | Egyptian Hieroglyph A001; Unicode scalar U+13000 |
| 𓀁 | U+13001 | Egyptian Hieroglyph A002 |
| 𓐷 | U+13437 | Egyptian Hieroglyph Vertical Joiner |
| 𓐸 | U+13438 | Egyptian Hieroglyph Horizontal Joiner |

**Subscripts:** Egyptological transliteration uses underdots, macrons, and sometimes subscript numerals in editorial conventions (e.g. phoneme distinctions); these are not hieroglyphic signs. No generalized hieroglyph subscript-letter alphabet exists.

**Diacritics and combining marks:** Scholarly transliteration uses characters such as ꜣ, ꜥ, ḥ, ḫ, and ṯ, while Unicode also provides combining diacritics. Preserve the edition’s transliteration standards and do not infer ancient vowels from inserted marks.

**Glyph strokes and layout:** Sign placement and orientation obey quadrat/layout conventions. Unicode format-control characters can indicate joining and grouping, but renderers vary; they do not encode brush stroke order or replace a sign-list reference such as Gardiner classification.

Unicode encodes characters, not the complete historical calligraphic or palaeographic process. Record source form, normalization, transliteration, and rendering assumptions separately.

# Evidence, dates, and comparison labels

This note explains what the seven extended profiles mean when they report an age, a root, a sibling, or a Unicode example. It prevents a reconstructed ancestor, a surviving text, a script, and a modern language from being treated as the same thing.

## How to read the dates

`BP` means years before 1950 CE. A date for a reconstructed ancestor is an inference, not an inscription date. `rangeBP` may summarize competing proposals or a model horizon; it is a confidence interval only when the cited study explicitly defines it that way. The `qualifyingAgeBP` value is the auditable value used for the minimum-age check, and the accompanying metadata states what that value dates.

Historical reconstruction and absolute dating are different operations. Comparative method can establish relative relationships and sequences of change; by itself it does not supply an absolute calendar date for a split. Absolute dates need an additional anchor, such as dated inscriptions or an explicitly described archaeological calibration. See the ANU discussion of the comparative method and absolute dating in [The Prehistory of Oceanic Languages](https://press.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/p69411/mobile/ch03.html).

## Seven profile evidence records

| Profile | Audited root value | What the value represents | Direct or documentary evidence |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Georgian | 3,950 BP | Low end of older comparative estimates for the Svan vs. Proto-Georgian-Zan split. A 2023 interdisciplinary model proposes a much older date above 12,500 BP; these are competing, method-dependent results, not a confidence interval. | Georgian inscriptions are conventionally attested from the fifth century CE. See the [2023 study and its discussion of model limitations](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-45500-w) and [Harvard's Georgian script history overview](https://daviscenter.fas.harvard.edu/research-initiatives/program-georgian-studies/cultural-highlights-georgia). |
| Khmer | 3,500 BP | Representative audit value within a contested 3,000–4,500 BP Proto-Austroasiatic model range; it is not a date for a Khmer inscription or an exact split. | Old Khmer inscriptional records are present by the early seventh century CE. See the [ANU Old Khmer grammar](https://openresearch-repository.anu.edu.au/bitstreams/ad26c181-b3e3-4776-b869-f37dd6c2a1a2/download) and [EFEO Corpus of Khmer Inscriptions](https://cik.efeo.fr/). |
| Hindi | 3,500 BP | Approximate Vedic/Indo-Aryan horizon used for the threshold audit. Proto-Indo-Aryan is reconstructed; the text-composition horizon is not a securely dated proto-language split. | The Ṛgveda is conventionally placed around 1500 BCE within a wider composition horizon, was transmitted orally, and survives in much later manuscripts. See [Cambridge's Sanskrit chapter](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/ancient-languages-of-asia-and-the-americas/sanskrit/CF7D5B91F9736880C0CECAC672754AEB). |
| Aramaic | 2,850 BP | Documentary benchmark for early Old Aramaic, not the date of the reconstructed Proto-Northwest Semitic split. | The Tell Fakhariya inscription is generally placed in the tenth–ninth centuries BCE, with the dating qualified. See [The Cambridge History of Iran](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/cambridge-history-of-iran/aramaic-in-the-achaemenian-empire/99EF05D99F450CEB6B1A2E24815FEB13) and [Encyclopaedia Iranica](https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/iran-vii10-aramaic/). |
| Proto-Oceanic | 3,200 BP | Archaeology-informed estimate for a reconstructed speech-community horizon. This is not a written attestation or a date produced by comparative method alone. | No contemporary Proto-Oceanic text or known native writing system exists; the language is reconstructed from descendants. See [ANU's current view of Oceanic prehistory](https://press.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/p69411/mobile/ch03.html) and [the Proto Oceanic lexicon's reconstruction method](https://tlopo.clld.org/contributions/5-1). |
| Ancient Egyptian | 8,000 BP | Younger edge of cited Proto-Afroasiatic chronology proposals. Published proposals extend from roughly 8,000–10,000 BP to 15,000 BP or older; no single date is consensus. | Egyptian is a later-attested daughter branch; Egyptian writing appears in the late fourth millennium BCE. See [Chicago's Egyptian chronology and script overview](https://isac.uchicago.edu/sites/default/files/uploads/shared/docs/oimp32.pdf) and the chronology discussion in [the Afroasiatic review](https://doi.org/10.4000/bmsap.564). |
| Mycenaean Greek / Linear B | 3,600 BP | Model-based Proto-Greek/early Greek horizon. It is separate from the date of extant Linear B tablets. | Mycenaean Greek documents in Linear B date mainly to about 1450–1150 BCE. The corpus notes that the tablets are mostly administrative and that Linear B underspecifies Greek phonology. See [DĀMOS](https://damos.hf.uio.no/about/content/) and [Unicode Standard, Chapter 8](https://www.unicode.org/versions/Unicode18.0.0/core-spec/chapter-8/). |

The values are therefore not seven equivalent kinds of “oldest record.” The `documentation` field in each JavaScript profile records that distinction as `epigraphic`, `oral-tradition`, or `none-known`, and stores separate source keys for that evidence.

## Language relationships are not script relationships

The `siblings` arrays are comparison sets and may mix close relatives, distant family members, dialect groups, or standardized registers. Each lineage note explains which relation applies. They should not be read as a claim that every listed item is an immediate sister branch.

Linear B is a writing system used to record Mycenaean Greek. Linear A is an earlier Aegean script whose language remains undeciphered; it is a script comparison, not a Greek language sibling. The profile stores that distinction under `relatedScripts` and keeps the language comparison set Greek-only.

Proto-Oceanic has no known native script. Its `*patu`, `ŋ`, `ā`, and `ʔ` samples are modern scholarly transcription characters, not recovered ancient glyphs.

## Unicode, glyphs, and writing practice

Unicode code points identify encoded characters. They do not specify the historical shape, pen or chisel strokes, stroke order, ductus, or manuscript allograph. Rendering may form a glyph from several code points or choose a contextual shape. For example, the Unicode Standard describes Khmer U+17D2 COENG as an invisible encoding component followed by a consonant in subscript sequences, and explains contextual glyph alternation in [Chapter 16](https://unicode.org/versions/Unicode18.0.0/core-spec/chapter-16/). It is not a standalone letter.

The validator checks that each listed sample reproduces its stated code points and that code points fall inside the documented Unicode script blocks. Proto-Oceanic is exempt from native-script block checks because its examples are explicitly transcription. These checks verify encoding metadata; they do not replace palaeographic review of dated artifacts.

## Family placement

Georgian is Kartvelian (South Caucasian), not Indo-European. The secure family comparison is with Svan and the Zan languages Mingrelian and Laz. Proto-Kartvelian is reconstructed from systematic correspondences; its date, homeland, and proposed links to archaeological cultures are debated. Ancient ethnonyms cannot be equated one-to-one with a modern language.

**Proposed root:** Proto-Kartvelian. The 2023 study summarizes older comparative estimates of 3,950–4,750 BP for the Svan vs. Proto-Georgian-Zan split and proposes a separate interdisciplinary model above 12,500 BP. The 3,950 BP audit value is the low end of the comparative estimates summarized by that study, not a consensus or direct attestation. The composite span is not a statistical confidence interval; the study notes limitations in uncertainty measurement and external validation for earlier calculations. Georgian inscriptions are conventionally attested from the fifth century CE, far later than the reconstructed family ancestor.

**Siblings and comparisons:**
- Mingrelian (Zan; close Kartvelian relative)
- Laz (Zan; close Kartvelian relative)
- Svan (separate Kartvelian branch)
- Judeo-Georgian varieties (Georgian-based ethnolects, not a separate family branch)

Do not flatten distant relatives and immediate sister groups into a single branching level.

## Chronology and evidence

Kartvelian prehistory is reconstructed, while Georgian becomes directly visible in inscriptions and manuscripts in Late Antiquity. The Georgian literary record is commonly dated from the fifth century CE; the earliest inscriptions and manuscript dates depend on the artifact and dating method. The centuries-long written tradition does not make modern Georgian unchanged from Proto-Kartvelian.

**Dating statement:** The 2023 study summarizes older comparative estimates of 3,950–4,750 BP for the Svan vs. Proto-Georgian-Zan split and proposes a separate interdisciplinary model above 12,500 BP. The 3,950 BP audit value is the low end of those comparative estimates, not consensus or direct attestation; the model results are not a statistical confidence interval.

Keep three clocks separate: (1) reconstructed ancestor age, (2) earliest surviving written attestation, and (3) emergence of a standardized modern variety. They answer different questions. A lack of early writing is not evidence that a language did not exist.

## Sound history

Kartvelian comparison includes rich consonant contrasts, ejectives, and complex consonant sequences. Georgian has stop series conventionally described by voicing and aspiration/ejective contrasts; exact phonetic descriptions vary by analysis and dialect. Sound correspondences must be stated as sets, not as universal letter substitutions. Vowel reduction, dialect contact, and historical borrowing complicate simple sound laws.

For reliable sound-change claims, identify the source stage, daughter branch, conditioning environment, and counterexamples. Orthographic similarity alone cannot establish cognacy or sound correspondence. Reconstructed segments use an asterisk and remain hypotheses.

## Syllables, prosody, and syntax

Georgian syllables permit substantial consonant clusters, especially across morpheme boundaries and in verb forms. Stress is generally weak and not the main grammatical signal; pitch and intonation require dialect-aware description. Constituent order is flexible, with case marking, agreement, and information structure shaping interpretation; a simple SVO label is inadequate for the full system.

The descriptive labels here are broad summaries, not templates for every dialect or genre. Compare attested forms by date and register; syntax may change while a writing convention remains conservative. Phonological syllables, script units, aksharas, and Unicode grapheme clusters are distinct analytical units.

## Script, Unicode, diacritics, and glyphs

Three Georgian scripts are historically recognized: Asomtavruli/Mrgvlovani, Nuskhuri, and Mkhedruli. Asomtavruli is the monumental/majuscule form; Nuskhuri is the more compact ecclesiastical minuscule, used with Asomtavruli in Khutsuri; Mkhedruli became the everyday civil hand and predominates today. Modern Mtavruli uppercase forms have separate Unicode encoding. Fifth-century inscriptions provide secure early evidence; claims of a pre-Christian alphabet remain disputed. Georgian scripts are historical systems, not merely font styles.

**Unicode model:** Georgian script encoding across Georgian U+10A0–U+10FF, Georgian Supplement U+2D00–U+2D2F, and Georgian Extended U+1C90–U+1CBF. Unicode encodes characters, not historical pen strokes or mandatory letterforms.

| Sample | Code points | Note |
|---|---|---|
| ა | U+10D0 | Mkhedruli a |
| Ⴀ | U+10A0 | Asomtavruli an |
| ⴀ | U+2D00 | Nuskhuri an |
| Ა | U+1C90 | Mtavruli an |

**Subscripts:** Georgian alphabetic spelling has no productive subscript-letter system.

**Diacritics and combining marks:** Modern standard spelling usually does not mark stress or tone with diacritics. Scholarly transliteration may use macrons, dots, or apostrophes; those belong to a declared transcription convention, not to ordinary Georgian Unicode spelling.

**Glyph strokes and layout:** Unicode scalar values identify characters; stroke order and regional glyph design are paleographic/font matters. Mkhedruli and Mtavruli have corresponding code points where encoded, while shaping and font support affect appearance.

Unicode encodes characters, not the complete historical calligraphic or palaeographic process. Record source form, normalization, transliteration, and rendering assumptions separately.
